# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

ripgrep can limit a search to certain kinds of files by name. Rather than
spelling out which file endings you want on every search, you name a *type*,
like `markdown` or `html`, and ripgrep looks only at the files that match. Four
flags cover this: `-t/--type` to include a type, `-T/--type-not` to leave one
out, `--type-add` to make your own, and `--type-list` to see what's on offer.

## See what's available: `--type-list`

Start here. Run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

You'll get every supported type, one per line: the type's name, a colon, then
the file-name patterns it stands for. ripgrep comes with a long list of
pre-defined types, and generally these correspond to well-known formats. To
pick one type out of the list, search the list itself:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

That tells you the `make` type covers Makefiles and `.mk` files. Some types
also have a short alias, so `markdown` and `md` name the same thing, and you
can use whichever you prefer.

## Search only one type: `-t/--type`

Once you know the name, pass it with `-t` (or the longer `--type`):

```
$ rg 'quarterly' --type markdown
```

or, more succinctly:

```
$ rg quarterly -tmarkdown
```

Both search for `quarterly` in Markdown files only, and skip everything else.
The value of a type is that a single name can stand for a broad range of file
endings. The `markdown` type, for instance, matches `.md` and `.markdown` and
several more, so you catch all of them at once without listing each ending
yourself.

You can name more than one type by repeating the flag. ripgrep then searches
files matching any of them:

```
$ rg quarterly -tmarkdown -thtml
```

## Leave a type out: `-T/--type-not`

The opposite of `-t` is `-T` (or `--type-not`). It searches everything *except*
the type you name:

```
$ rg 'quarterly' --type-not html
```

or:

```
$ rg quarterly -Thtml
```

That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files
of this type." You can mix the two in one command. Include one type, exclude
another:

```
$ rg quarterly -tmarkdown -Thtml
```

## Make your own type: `--type-add`

If ripgrep has no type for the files you care about, or you want to group
several endings under one name, define your own with `--type-add`. Give it a
name, a colon, and a pattern:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines a type called `web` for `.html`, `.css`, and `.js` files, then
applies it with `-tweb` and searches for `title`. Run `--type-list` alongside
it and your `web` type shows up in the list, even though it isn't one of
ripgrep's built-in types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
```

Two things to know. First, a type name may contain only letters and numbers, no
spaces or punctuation. Second, `--type-add` only applies to the command you run
it in. ripgrep doesn't save it anywhere. If you want a type available in every
search, you can work around this by either creating a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or adding the same `--type-add` line to your ripgrep configuration file, so
every search picks it up.

You can also build a type out of types you already have. The special `include`
directive pulls in the patterns from one or more other type names, separated by
commas:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:html,css,js' -tsrc title
```

## The special `all` type

Both `-t` and `-T` accept the value `all`. `--type all` searches only the files
ripgrep recognizes as *some* type, a "whitelist" search:

```
$ rg quarterly --type all
```

`--type-not all` does the reverse. It searches only files ripgrep does *not*
recognize, a "blacklist" search:

```
$ rg quarterly --type-not all
```

So a file with no extension, which no type matches, is searched by
`--type-not all` and skipped by `--type all`.

## One note on precedence

Note that type filters have lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and than
any rules found in ignore files. If a glob or an ignore rule has already decided
a file's fate, a type flag won't override it. You'll rarely notice this in
everyday use, but it explains the odd case where a file you expected to see
doesn't turn up.
